items.title: Are VPNs Safe? What Has Gone Wrong, What Has Held Up
items.summary: A VPN from a company with a checkable record is safe to use, and legal in most countries. The risk is the company itself, because it sees the traffic you’re hiding from everyone else. That’s the trade at the heart of every VPN. Your internet provider, the café Wi-Fi and the sites you visit see less, and one company sees more. Most of the time that company keeps its word. Sometimes it hasn’t, and both kinds of story are on the public record: court files, police searches, leaked databases, audit reports. They tell you more than any “military-grade encryption” badge on a download page. New to VPNs? Start with what a VPN is and whether you need one .

items.title: Do You Need a VPN? An Honest Answer for Each Situation
items.summary: Not for everyday browsing at home. You need one when the network you’re on shouldn’t see where you go, or blocks where you want to go. That covers fewer situations than VPN ads suggest, and a few more than the skeptics admit. Almost every site now encrypts what you send, so the old picture of a stranger reading your bank password over café Wi-Fi is mostly out of date. What’s left is quieter: the café, the hotel, your internet provider or a government can still see which sites you visit, and some of them block the ones you need. The table gives the short answer for each case. The chapters below explain them, name the free tools that do some of these jobs better, and work out whether a VPN is worth paying for. If you’re not sure what a VPN does in the first place, start with what a VPN is . Your situation Does a VPN help Hotel, airport or café Wi-Fi Yes Or use mobile data. The network’s owner, and any fake copy of it, can’t see which sites you visit. Keeping your browsing from your internet provider Yes It sees a VPN server, not the sites. A country that blocks sites or apps Yes, where legal Install it before you travel; some countries block VPN companies too. Your streaming service or bank from abroad Usually Services block the VPN addresses they find. Torrenting Yes Other peers see the server’s address, not yours. Banking and shopping at home No HTTPS already encrypts it. Hackers, scams and malware No Updates, a password manager and passkeys do that. Staying anonymous No The VPN company and every site you log in to know you. Tor comes closer. An internet shutdown No When the connection is cut, there’s nothing to tunnel through. The rule behind every row: a VPN hides where you go from the network you’re on. It does nothing about who you are once you log in. Sources: FTC, Australian Cyber Security Centre and the chapters below. Checked November 22, 2026.

items.title: Backblaze Now Lists Purchase and Location Data Among What It Shares for Targeted Ads
items.summary: Backblaze, the cloud backup company, now says it has “sold or shared” four kinds of its customers’ personal information for targeted advertising, purchase records and location data among them. The list is in a rewritten privacy notice that takes effect on 1 December 2026. Backblaze announced it by email on 20 November; PrivacyAffairs’ editor, Miklos Zoltan, is a customer and got one. It says the notice was “updated to improve clarity and organization, and to reflect current legal requirements,” lists new data processing agreements, an updated Cookie Notice and subprocessor list, and tells customers “no action is required.” It doesn’t mention advertising or the opt-out. Customers started arguing over it on Reddit and Hacker News on Saturday, and a second Hacker News thread was on the site’s front page as we published. Neowin covered it on 21 November. We found no coverage by larger outlets. Part of the alarm is misplaced, and part of it isn’t. We compared the new notice with the version it replaces, with Backblaze’s 2023 notice for California residents and with the tracking set-up of its website. Two of the four categories were already being shared with ad networks in 2023, at least for Californians. Purchase and location data are new, and so is telling every customer about it. The files you back up are a separate matter.

items.title: What Is a VPN? How It Works and What It Won’t Hide
items.summary: A VPN (virtual private network) is a service that sends your internet traffic through an encrypted tunnel to a server run by the VPN company. Websites then see that server’s IP address, not yours. That one change cuts both ways. Your internet provider, and whoever runs the Wi-Fi you’re on, can no longer see which sites you visit. The VPN company now can, a detail most explanations leave out. The word also covers two different things. At work, a VPN connects your laptop into the company network so you can reach internal systems from home; that’s the original meaning, and the one in NIST’s definitions . The VPN apps people buy for privacy, travel and streaming use the same kind of tunnel the other way round, taking you out onto the internet from somewhere else. This guide is about the second kind. For the work kind, your IT team has the answers.

items.title: A brief history of syslog timestamps, (Sun, Nov 22nd)
items.summary: BLUF: Debian and Ubuntu dropped a config directive in the rsyslogd package in early 2023. As any of my FOR577 students will tell you, I'm a fan of ISO-8601 (ok, RFC 3339, too, see below). They'll probably also tell you I'm a firm believer in UTC||GTFO especially on servers (also true, and I've made stickers to prove it). I was also asked recently why the syslog timestamps in newer Ubuntu and Debian systems changed to ISO-8601 (well, probably actually RFC 3339, but I won't got down that rabbithole in this handler's diary) timestamps from the historical Mmm dd hh:mm:ss format we've known since the 1980s. I had noticed the same, a few years ago, but never really paid attention to it. Given the question from a student, I decided to do a little research on the subject and this diary is the result. To back up some, the syslog protocol and syslogd were originally the creation of Eric Allman in 1983 because he needed a way to debug sendmail[ 1 ]. They became part of BSD 4.2 that same year. BSD 4.2 also happened to be my introduction to Unix in 1983. Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2 major branches of Unix at the time. System V adopted the protocol and routing interfaces but built the daemon on top of System V internals. The first effort to develop the protocol into an actual standard was an IETF draft in Oct 2000 that evolved into RFC 3164[ 2 ] in 2001, by which time the protocol was actually already 18 years old. This is the syslog message format we've all come to know so well over the years. Meanwhile, around 2005, rsyslogd added the option of outputing RFC 3339 timestamps. In 2009, RFC 3164 was superceded by RFC 5424[ 3 ] which defined the timestamp to be of the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss]Z or YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss](+/-)hh:mm . Despite the new RFC, the default setting even for rsyslogd in most Linux distros continued to be to write messages to the log files in the older format (referred to as the BSD format, as specified in the title of RFC 3164), by setting a directive in /etc/rsyslog.conf (the RSYSLOG_TraditionalFileFormat directive). That brings us to 2023, with the release of Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 23.04 (not a LTS release) both distros stopped installing rsyslogd by default and defaulted to the systemd journal for logging and removed the directive from the default config file for those who did install it.. Many system administrators continue to install rsyslogd because they had infrastructure in place for forwarding syslog to central log servers and/or SIEMs. These are the folks most likely to have noticed the format change. Meanwhile, Fedora and Alma (and presumably the rest of the RedHat family) have left the directive in place when the package is installed. From a Ubuntu 24.04 system: From a Fedora 44 system: Meanwhile you can get either one with journalctl by setting the output format to either short (BSD format) or short-iso-precise (ISO format). Also, note that rsyslogd is not the only option for a syslog server. I've been using syslog-ng as the syslog server on my home log collector since about 2000. In syslog-ng, the new 'ISO' timestamps can be enabled by setting the following two options in syslog-ng.conf: ts-format(iso) and frac-digits(6) . Since I have just been upgrading my central log server for years, I haven't done a fresh install lately, so I'm not sure if that is the default. I had to explicitly add it to my config. References: 1. The History of Centralized Logging 2. RFC 3164: The BSD Syslog Protocol 3. RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol --------------- Jim Clausing, GIAC GSE #26 jclausing --at-- isc [dot] sans (dot) edu (c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

items.title: Signal Is Blocking AI Agents From Reading Your Screen
items.summary: Signal is blocking OS-level AI agents from reading its app on iOS 27 and Android, warning that Gemini and Siri AI threaten its privacy guarantees. Signal is restricting new AI agents built into iOS 27 and Android from capturing its data, president Meredith Whittaker announced. The company already did something similar on Windows last year, blocking screenshots to stop Microsoft’s Recall from capturing Signal messages by default. Now it’s doing the same wherever it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the Signal screen. The process is simple, but it raises serious privacy concerns. Operating system-level AI agents, such as Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI, scan the content displayed on your screen so they can answer questions and perform tasks for you. This means these AI agents can capture your Signal data and use it to answer your questions and carry out your requests. “In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.” reads the announcement . “The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” Signal’s security model is based on open-source code and encryption that has been formally checked and reviewed by independent researchers for more than a decade. However, this protection can’t help if an AI agent reads your messages directly from the screen before encryption becomes relevant. Once captured, the data may be stored in a local database or sent to a remote server used by the AI agent, completely outside Signal’s control. Google, Apple, and Microsoft aren’t just three companies among many here. “these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem.” continues the report. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy.” When the ocean starts working against the fish swimming in it, the fish can’t simply find a different ocean. Signal’s fix is narrow: block screenshots on iOS 27, and block AI assistant screen capture attempts on Android. Users can turn the protection off in settings if they want to take screenshots, but doing so exposes their messages, and their contacts’ messages, to the same agents Signal is trying to keep out. The company is upfront that this doesn’t close every door, since an agent could still reach app data through the filesystem rather than the screen. MacOS gets no protection at all right now, because Apple and Microsoft don’t give developers a clean way to block AI access without wrecking the normal user experience. Signal says it spent real engineering time just doing forensic work across Android and iOS to figure out what these AI systems actually do with app data, because the documentation isn’t there. That’s a strange place for a company Signal’s size to be: reverse-engineering the privacy behavior of the platforms it depends on. Signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft to take two specific steps. First, they should give app developers a clear way to prevent AI agents from accessing their data, including information on the screen, files, notifications, and APIs. Second, they should explain exactly how these AI agents access, collect, and process user data. Signal also raises concerns about third-party AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which can use accessibility permissions that users originally granted for other purposes. The company adds that confidential computing doesn’t solve the problem because the platform still controls the privacy decision, not the app developer or the user. Signal says it’s already talking with Google and Apple about better support for apps that handle sensitive information. The company is cautiously optimistic, but whether these discussions lead to real changes will depend on what the two companies actually do over the coming year. Signal frames the stakes plainly for anyone tempted to see this as one company’s problem. “We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data.” the report cocludes. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Signal)

items.title: GL.iNet Owners Find a Second Backdoor on Their Routers, Some Planted in 2025
items.summary: Owners checking their GL.iNet routers for Friday’s cloud attack have found a separate, older backdoor, on some routers since the autumn of 2025. It isn’t in GL.iNet’s security notice of 20 November, and the check GL.iNet tells owners to run doesn’t find it. It starts with the router, reports to servers named to look like AdGuard and OpenWrt, and survives firmware updates that keep the settings. The scale is not small. RemoteToHome Consulting, which sets up GL.iNet VPN routers for remote workers, says it found the backdoor installed and running on 47 of the 183 routers it has checked since Saturday. On Sunday morning, a GL.iNet staff member listed it among the reports the company is looking at, without saying more. When we published, the find had been discussed only on GL.iNet’s forum and in two community projects on GitHub. We found no news coverage. Our report on the 20 November incident covers the cloud attack itself.

items.title: SECURITY AFFAIRS AI-CYBERSECURITY NEWSLETTER ROUND 9
items.summary: Security Affairs AI-CYBERSECURITY newsletter includes a collection of the best articles and research on AI in the international landscape Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing cybersecurity, reshaping both the techniques used by attackers and the tools available to defenders. AI agents can automate tasks, analyze large amounts of data, discover vulnerabilities and accelerate offensive operations. items.title: Mojang Used Hobby Scanners to Find Private Minecraft Servers, Developer Says
items.summary: Mojang has been finding private Minecraft servers through hobbyists’ internet scanners and blocking them over crude server descriptions, says the developer of one of those scanners. Part of her account can be checked against Mojang’s own blocklist. We tested every IPv4 address against it: 91 entries are plain IP addresses, 71 of them added since early August, and 25 of those belong to home internet providers such as Spectrum, AT&T and Swisscom. None of the 25 was on the list before August. The developer, who goes by Evelien and posts as sipacid, published her story on Saturday, 21 November, under the title “ port scanning for mojang “. Her Bluesky post about it had 114 likes and 41 reposts by 00:55 UTC on Sunday. It also sits on Hacker News and Lobsters, with little discussion so far, and we found no coverage in major outlets.
